title: Design Principles in Practice: SOLID Principles

blocks.text: Imagine a world where software is easy to change, extend, and maintain. The SOLID design principles are key to making this a reality.

blocks.markdown: The SOLID principles are a set of five design principles intended to make software designs more understandable, flexible, and maintainable. These principles help ensure that software components are properly encapsulated, decoupled, and adhere to a clear contract.

blocks.title: SOLID Principles
blocks.text: SOLID stands for Single Responsibility, Open-Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion principles.

blocks.markdown: Let's explore each of these principles, starting with the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP).

blocks.title: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
blocks.text: A class should have only one reason to change, meaning it should have only one job or responsibility.

blocks.title: Identifying SRP Violation
blocks.prompt: Consider a class `Report` that both generates a report and sends it via email. How does this violate SRP?

steps.text: Identify the responsibilities in the `Report` class.
The `Report` class has two responsibilities: generating the report and sending it via email.
Since it has more than one responsibility, it violates the SRP.

blocks.answer: The `Report` class violates SRP because it handles both report generation and email sending.

blocks.markdown: Next, consider the Open-Closed Principle (OCP), which states that software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.

blocks.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
blocks.text: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without affecting the correctness of the program.

blocks.title: LSP Violation Example
blocks.prompt: Suppose we have a class `Bird` with a method `fly()`. A subclass `Penguin` inherits from `Bird` but cannot fly. How does this violate LSP?

steps.text: Identify the superclass and subclass relationship.
The `Penguin` class inherits from `Bird` but cannot fulfill the `fly()` method of `Bird`.
This substitution of `Bird` with `Penguin` violates LSP because it changes expected behavior.

blocks.answer: The `Penguin` class violates LSP because it cannot fulfill the `fly()` method of its superclass `Bird`.

blocks.markdown: The Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) suggests that no client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use.

blocks.title: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
blocks.text: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.

rows: A class should have only one reason to change.
Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.
Objects should be replaceable with instances of their subtypes without altering the correctness.
Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.
Depend on abstractions, not on concretions.
blocks.caption: Summary of SOLID Principles

blocks.markdown: By adhering to these principles, you can create software that is easier to maintain and extend over time.

points: SOLID principles guide the design of maintainable and flexible software.
Each principle addresses a specific aspect of software design, such as responsibility, substitution, and dependency.
